title: How Police Sketches Work
summary: Josh and Chuck promote their animated web series, then explore how police sketches work. They cover the Oklahoma City bombing suspect Timothy McVeigh, whose police sketch helped catch him after a traffic stop, and the history of sketching from Annibale Carracci and Alphonse Bertillon's criminal anthropometry. They describe the forensic artist's interview process (report building, free recall, recognition, and collaborative sketching), tools like Identikit and computer composites, and the FBI finding that hand-drawn sketches are more accurate. They discuss why eyewitness memory is unreliable, age progression and facial reconstruction, and the value of sketches even when imperfect. The episode closes with listener mail from Luke about laughing so hard during an earlier episode that he was injured.

segments.title: Opening banter and animated web series promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote a new animated web series of shorts released weekly on the website, then banter about the studio and the day's mood.

segments.title: Timothy McVeigh and the sketch that led to his arrest
segments.summary: McVeigh was pulled over for a traffic violation within two hours of the Oklahoma City bombing. While in custody, a police sketch circulated and a highway patrol officer recognized it as resembling him, which helped identify him as the bomber.

segments.title: Quality of police sketches and history of sketching
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how many police sketches are poor, with humorous collections online, and mention the literary character sketches. They tell the story of the sixteenth-century painter Annibale Carracci sketching robbers, and note that modern police sketching developed around the time of Jack the Ripper.

segments.title: Alphonse Bertillon and criminal anthropometry
segments.summary: Criminologist Alphonse Bertillon measured criminals' physical features to create criminal anthropometry, used to identify repeat offenders in France before reliable fingerprinting. This led people to consider sketching suspects, and Bertillon also appears in the crime scene photography work.

segments.title: Who makes police sketches: officers, contractors, and staff artists
segments.summary: Forensic artists may be patrol officers who draw well, civilian contractors, or full-time staff. There is no official university degree, but training exists through the FBI and private courses. Art correspondence courses are mentioned.

segments.title: The four-part sketch interview process
segments.summary: The interview is described in parts: rapport building, free recall where witnesses describe features (often starting with hair or head shape), specific questioning and using mugshots or celebrity comparisons, and collaborative refinement where the sketch develops details.

segments.title: Identikit, composites, and hand-drawn versus computer sketches
segments.summary: Identikit, introduced in the United States in 1969 by the Townsend Corporation, used transparent overlays of facial features. Composites combine multiple witness accounts. Computer software is used by some, but the FBI found hand-drawn sketches about four percent more likely to be accurate. Stephen Mancusi of the NYPD and Roderick Scratchard of Philadelphia are named.

segments.title: Accuracy statistics for police sketches
segments.summary: Hosts note that hand-drawn sketches are recognizable about nine percent of the time and computer ones about five percent, based on comparing sketches with later-caught suspects. They say sketches still provide leads and publicity.

segments.title: Why eyewitness memory is unreliable
segments.summary: Recognition memory works on whole faces, while recall requires detail. Stress, speed, lack of consolidation, memory infiltration from movies, poor eyesight, age over sixty, and distance all reduce witness accuracy. Convenience store height markers are mentioned. DNA phenotyping is noted as a promising but early tool.

segments.title: Age progression, facial reconstruction, and sign-off with listener mail
segments.summary: Forensic artists also create age progressed images and facial reconstructions from remains. Hosts note the Chinese state TV animations and close with a listener mail from Luke about laughing so hard he was injured in an emergency room visit, followed by contact information.
